The Criminal Investigations Department has launched an investigation following the discovery of missing cocaine exhibits kept in the custody of the Suva High Court.

7 cocaine bars missing from Suva High Court Exhibit Room By Vijay Narayan 16/09/2026 Suva High Court The Criminal Investigations Department has launched an investigation following the discovery of missing cocaine exhibits kept in the custody of the Suva High Court. fijivillage News was alerted early this week about cocaine from Joshua Aziz Rahman's case allegedly missing from the Suva Court House. We had then asked Police and the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions. The Office of the DPP said they were not aware of the allegations but we should check with Police as they are responsible for exhibits including storing and securing drugs. We were told on Monday night that the drugs were not missing. However Assistant Commissioner of Police Crime Loraini Seru now says a physical check of the exhibits was conducted on Tuesday, in the presence of senior judiciary officials, a senior official from the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, Police and an officer from the Crime Scene Investigations (CSI) capturing the inspection process. It was discovered that the exhibits linked to a high-profile drug case had allegedly been tampered with. It was also discovered that seven bars were missing from the initial thirty-nine exhibited to the Suva High Court Exhibit Room. Investigations are underway by a team from the CID. The Supreme Court had earlier restored Fiji-Canadian national Joshua Aziz Rahman’s conviction and sentence imposed by the High Court over the 39.5kg of cocaine worth $31 million found at a Caubati home in 2019. The High Court sentenced Rahman to 23 years imprisonment in October 2021, with a non-parole period of 14 years, following his conviction. Stay with us for developments.

BREAKING : All cocaine bars worth $31 million tampered with and missing from the Suva High Court Exhibit Room Flour found in remaining 'cocaine' bars in the room By Vijay Narayan 29/09/2026 A major development this afternoon as fijivillage News can now confirm that all the cocaine bars weighing 39.5kg and worth $31 million from Fiji-Canadian national Joshua Aziz Rahman's case have been tampered with and the bars in the Suva High Court Exhibit Room do not contain cocaine. This means that 39 bars of cocaine are now missing. We have been told that the 32 remaining bars that were in the exhibit room was filled with flour. fijivillage News has been following this issue for a few weeks after serious concerns being raised about how drug exhibits are being stored, and the procedures surrounding that. While answering our questions, Police have today confirmed that forensic tests conducted on the remaining drug exhibits have all returned negative which means that it is not cocaine. Police confirm that the exhibits have all been tampered with and the investigation is focused on those directly charged with the management of the exhibits at the High Court Registry in Suva. A person of interest allegedly involved in this shocking incident is currently overseas, and Police say the person will be questioned. Two weeks ago, the Criminal Investigations Department launched an investigation following the discovery of missing cocaine exhibits kept in the custody of the Suva High Court. fijivillage News was alerted earlier this month about the missing cocaine. We had then asked Police and the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions. The Office of the DPP said they were not aware of the allegations but we should check with Police as they are responsible for exhibits including storing and securing drugs. We were told on the 14th of this month that the drugs were not missing. However, Assistant Commissioner of Police Crime Loraini Seru said on the 16th of this month that a physical check of the exhibits was conducted on the 15th, in the presence of senior judiciary officials, a senior official from the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, Police and an officer from the Crime Scene Investigations (CSI) capturing the inspection process. It was discovered that the exhibits linked to a high-profile drug case had allegedly been tampered with. It was also discovered that seven bars were missing from the initial thirty-nine exhibited to the Suva High Court Exhibit Room. The Supreme Court had earlier restored Fiji-Canadian national Joshua Aziz Rahman's conviction and sentence imposed by the High Court over the 39.5kg of cocaine worth $31 million found at a Caubati home in 2019. The High Court sentenced Rahman to 23 years imprisonment in October 2021, with a non-parole period of 14 years, following his conviction. We have asked Police whether the person who removed the cocaine bars from the High Court Exhibit Room has been identified, and whether the person is an employee of the Judicial Department. We have asked whether CCTV cameras were placed where the drugs went missing and whether the person fled the country. fijivillage News has also asked for comments from Police on why the cocaine was still in storage after Joshua Aziz Rahman was sentenced in 2021 and why the drug was not destroyed after the case. We have also asked when the High Court knew that the drugs were missing. Chief Justice Salesi Temo had earlier said the prosecution failed to apply for the destruction of 39.5kg of cocaine during the early stages of the drug case. He said those responsible for the missing exhibits will be taken to task. Stay with us for developments.

CJ Temo confirms several measures being implemented after missing cocaine from High Court Exhibit Room No comments on whether full audit and tests of all drugs in the exhibit rooms will be conducted By Vijay Narayan 02/10/2026 Chief Justice Salesi Temo has today confirmed that the judiciary is implementing measures after the disappearance of about $50 million worth of cocaine fromÂ two cases between March and September this year.

He confirms that a comprehensive security assessment of court premises nationwide is being done after the incidents at the Suva High Court Exhibit Room; a review of exhibit handling, storage, retention, and destruction procedures; upgrades to physical security infrastructure, including enhanced access control systems for sensitive and restricted areas; expansion and enhancement of CCTV coverage and monitoring capabilities within court facilities; strengthening chain-of-custody requirements and accountability measures for exhibits; a review of staff access privileges, registry controls, and security protocols; additional training and awareness programs for staff responsible for exhibit management and security; and the development of enhanced audit, compliance, and oversight mechanisms to strengthen accountability and transparency.

Chief Justice Temo says the judiciary is also assessing opportunities to modernise registry operations through improved technology, strengthened records management systems, enhanced inventory controls, and other measures designed to reduce risk and improve operational integrity.

He says public confidence in the judiciary is fundamental to the rule of law, and while the reported disappearance of exhibits is a matter of serious concern, it is equally important that the response is measured, professional, and focused on ensuring that such incidents cannot be repeated.

He says the judiciary views this matter with the utmost seriousness and is committed to ensuring that the facts are thoroughly established through the proper investigative process.

The Chief Justice says at the same time, they are taking decisive steps to strengthen security systems, modernise exhibit management practices, and enhance accountability across all court facilities.

He says they will continue to work closely with the Fiji Police Force and other relevant stakeholders to ensure that any deficiencies identified are addressed promptly and comprehensively.

Chief Justice Temo says as investigations remain active, it would be inappropriate to comment further on matters that may become the subject of criminal proceedings.

He confirms the judiciary is providing its full cooperation to the Fiji Police Force as investigations continue.

The Chief Justice says court officials have been directed to make available all relevant records, documentation, and information required by investigators, and the judiciary remains committed to supporting a thorough, transparent, and independent investigation.

He adds at this stage, the Police have advised that a number of persons of interest have been identified however, it is important to note that the concept of the rule of law, imported from Great Britain since the Deed of Cession in 1874, demands that persons of interest, are treated fairly within the four corners of the law.

Chief Justice Temo says that means that every person, who may later be accused of a crime, are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt, in a court of law; not in the court of social media.

He says should the investigation establish sufficient evidence of criminal wrongdoing, it will be for the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions to independently determine whether charges are to be laid.

The Chief Justice says if charges are laid by the Director of Public Prosecutions, the judiciary will ensure that the trial is carried out within a reasonable time, that is, a timeline under 2 years.

He says all due processes will be observed for the prosecution and the defence.

He adds at the conclusion of the trial, the appeal process will also be streamlined, a timeline of 12 months.

Chief Justice Temo says this matter is deeply concerning.

He says court exhibits are an integral part of the administration of justice and the integrity of criminal proceedings.

He adds their secure custody, management, and preservation are essential to ensuring fair trials, protecting the rights of all parties, maintaining public confidence in the justice system, and upholding the rule of law.

fijivillage News has asked Chief Justice Temo on whether a full audit will be conducted at all court exhibit rooms, and whether all the drug exhibits will be tested to confirm that they are actually drugs. He has not responded to this.Â

Police investigations continue into the cases of the missing cocaine from the Suva Court House.

Man allegedly linked to missing cocaine exhibits being questioned by CID Sister of Acting Head of independent institution wanted for questioning By Vijay Narayan 03/10/2026 Police investigators continue to question an individual believed to have been involved in the tampering of the drug exhibits at the Suva High Court. It has been confirmed that the individual is closely linked to one of the six persons of interest directly charged with the management of exhibits. The six are from the Judicial Department. He is currently being questioned at the Criminal Investigations Department Headquarters. Meanwhile investigations continue with regards to the involvement of other persons of interest. One of the persons of interest is the sister of an Acting Head of an independent institution. The woman who was working at the Judicial Department is overseas, and questions are being raised on how she managed to go abroad. When questioned, Police Commissioner, Rusiate Tudravu says they will not reveal which country this person went to as she could have gone somewhere else after that. He also did not want to confirm anything and said to allow the investigation process to take its course. Chief Justice Salesi Temo and Chief Registrar Tomasi Bainivalu say they will let the investigation process take its course. Stay with us for developments.

The Constitution Amendment Bill proposes the retention of a 55 member Parliament however a system is proposed where 33 constituency members or such number as Parliament may by written law

Bill proposes retention of 55 member Parliament - 33 constituency members and 22 party list members 5 year Parliament term proposed in Bill By Vijay Narayan 30/09/2026 The Constitution Amendment Bill proposes the retention of a 55 member Parliament however a system is proposed where 33 constituency members or such number as Parliament may by written law prescribe, which includes 5 maritime constituencies chosen directly by the registered voters of those constituencies in a first-past-the-post election; and 22 party list members or such number as Parliament may by written law prescribe, allocated to political parties in proportion to the total number of votes for the candidates of that party in the constituency seats. Parliament or the House of Representatives is to be composed in a manner that reflects, as closely as practicable, the proportion of votes cast for political parties. A political party is entitled to proportional representation if it secures not less than 5 percent of the party vote. Constituency seats won are deducted from each party’s proportional entitlement, with the balance filled from party lists. The Party list seats must be allocated in accordance with a written law prescribing an appropriate mathematical rounding method, which rounds fractions to whole numbers to determine seat allocations. Candidates unaffiliated with a political party may contest constituency seats, and if elected, serve as independent members without affecting proportional allocation. A candidate of a party can stand for election in a constituency seat and be included in the party’s list for a party list seat. Parliament may provide, by written law, for temporary special measures relating to the way in which party lists must be constituted, for example measures to ensure, as far as possible, equal numbers of male and female candidates; or measures to otherwise facilitate diverse representation on party lists. The maritime constituencies are Rotuma, Yasawa, Kadavu, Lomaiviti and Lau. A candidate for election to the House of Representatives must be either nominated by a registered political party or nominated as an independent candidate in accordance with the laws governing elections. A person may be a candidate for election to the House of Representatives only if the person is a citizen of Fiji; is qualified to be registered as a voter and is registered on the Register of Voters; is ordinarily resident in Fiji for at least 2 years immediately before being nominated; is not an undischarged bankrupt; is not a member of the Electoral Commission and has not been a member of that Commission at any time during the 4 years immediately before being nominated; is not subject to a sentence of imprisonment when nominated; has not, at any time during the 8 years immediately before being nominated, been convicted of an offence under any law for which the maximum penalty is a term of imprisonment of 12 months or more; and has not, in the 5 years immediately before being nominated, been found guilty of any offence under a law relating to elections, registration of political parties or registration of voters. The total number of candidates that a political party may nominate for any general election must not be more than the total number of seats in the House of Representatives, and the total number of candidates that a political party may nominate for any by-election must not be more than the total number of vacant seats in the House of Representatives for which the by-election is held. If a seat in the House of Representatives becomes vacant, the vacancy must be filled in the case of a constituency seat, by a by-election; and in the case of a party list seat, by the next candidate on the party list; or if there is no next candidate on the party list, by a by-election. The Bill also proposes the House of Representatives continues for 5 years from the date of its firstmeeting after a general election of the members of the House of Representatives, unless sooner dissolved in accordance with the Constitution.

Constitution Amendment Bill proposes Fijian to continue as common name Religious freedom guaranteed, State and all persons holding public office must treat all religions equally By Vijay Narayan 30/09/2026 The Constitution Amendment Bill tabled in parliament today proposes all citizens of Fiji are to continue to be known as Fijians, and Indigenous Fijians may be referred to as iTaukeinivanua o Viti. The Bill tabled by parliament also says that the Republic of Fiji is a sovereign democratic State founded on the values of Christianity and family values; respect for human rights, freedom and the rule of law; an independent, impartial, competent and accessible system of justice; equality for all and care for the less fortunate based on the values in the Bill of Rights; human dignity, respect for the individual, personal integrity and responsibility, civic involvement and mutual support; good governance, including the limitation and separation of powers; transparency and accountability; common and equal citizenry and national unity; and a prudent, efficient and sustainable relationship with nature. The Bill says although religion and the State are separate, the people of the Republic of Fiji acknowledge that worship and reverence for God are the source of good governance and leadership. It also states that religious liberty is a founding principle of the State, religious belief is personal and that religious liberty means the State and all persons holding public office must treat all religions equally; the State and all persons holding public office must not dictate any religious belief; the State and all persons holding public office must not prefer or advance, by any means, any particular religion, religious denomination, religious belief, or religious practice over another, or over any non-religious belief; and no person may assert any religious belief as a legal reason to disregard this Constitution or any other written law. Citizens of Fiji may also hold multiple citizenship , which means that upon accepting the citizenship of a foreign country, a person remains a citizen of Fiji unless he or she renounces that status; a former citizen of Fiji, who lost that citizenship upon acquiring foreign citizenship, may regain citizenship of Fiji, while retaining that foreign citizenship unless the laws of that foreign country provide otherwise; and upon becoming a citizen of Fiji, a foreign person may retain his or her existing citizenship unless the laws of that foreign country provide otherwise. The Constitution Amendment Bill also states that any attempt to establish a Government other than in compliance with this Constitution is unlawful, and anything done to further that attempt is invalid and of no force or effect; and no immunities can lawfully be granted under any law to any person. The Bill also states that every person has the right to free early childhood education; free primary and secondary education; and free further education for persons who were unable to complete their primary and secondary education. It also says conversational and contemporary iTaukei, Rotuman and Hindi languages must be taught in all primary schools. The State may also direct any educational institution to teach subjects pertaining to health, civic education and issues of national interest, and any educational institution must comply with any such directions made by the State.

Bill proposes that Bose Levu Vakaturaga should appoint President and Vice President after consultation with PM By Vijay Narayan 30/09/2026 The Constitution Amendment Bill proposes that Fiji's President and Vice-President are to be appointed by the Bose Levu Vakaturaga after consultation with the Prime Minister. The President and Vice-President hold office for 4 years, and each is eligible for re-appointment for one further term of 4 years, but is not eligible for re-appointment after that. A person is qualified to be appointed to the office of the President or the Vice-President only if the person has had a distinguished career in any aspect of national or international life, whether in the public or private sector; is a citizen of Fiji; is not a member of a political party; is not a candidate for election to any other office in the State; and is not under sentence or subject to be sentenced for an offence punishable by a term of imprisonment of 12 months or more. The Constitution Amendment Bill will be debated in Parliament on Friday. Under the 2013 Constitution, the President is chosen by Parliament after nominations by the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition. There is no Vice President, and the Chief Justice acts as the President when the President is out of the country. Under the 1997 Constitution, the President and Vice President were appointed by the Boselevu Vakaturaga.

23-member Senate proposed to review Bills By Mansi Chand 30/09/2026 The Constitution Amendment Bill proposes the establishment of a 23-member Senate, which will be responsible for reviewing Bills passed by the House of Representatives.

It states that 14 Senators will be appointed by the President on the advice of the Bose Levu Vakaturaga, six on the advice of the Prime Minister, two on the advice of the Leader of the Opposition and one on the advice of the Rotuma Island Council.

The Bill states that appointments recommended by the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition must reflect Fiji’s diversity, including descendants of Girmitiyas and other minority groups.

The Bill says if the position of Leader of the Opposition is vacant when appointments are being made, the Prime Minister will take on the role of the Opposition Leader in relation to the two appointments allocated to that office.

It says a person will only be eligible to become a Senator if they are also eligible to stand as a candidate for election to the House of Representatives.

The term of the Senate will end when the term of the House of Representatives expires or if the House is dissolved earlier.

A Senator’s seat will become vacant if they die or resign, are convicted of an offence punishable by 12 months or more imprisonment, cease to be eligible to contest a House of Representatives election, are absent from two consecutive Senate sittings without permission, or are nominated as a candidate for the House of Representatives.

The members of the Senate must, at its first sitting after a general election for members of the House of Representatives and whenever the office of President of the Senate is vacant, elect from their members a President of the Senate.

A person elected as President of the Senate must make an oath before the Secretary General to the Senate.

The members of the Senate must, at their first sitting after a general election for members of the House of Representatives and whenever the office of Vice-President of the Senate is vacant, elect one of their members as Vice-President of the Senate.

The Vice-President of the Senate must perform the duties of President of the Senate if the President of the Senate is absent from duty or from Fiji or is, for any other reason, unable to perform those duties.

It states if neither the President nor the Vice-President is able to perform the duties of the Senate, the members of the Senate must elect one of their members to preside at meetings of the Senate.

The office of President of the Senate does not become vacant on the expiry of the term of the Senate but becomes vacant on the day immediately before the first sitting of the Senate after a general election for members of the House of Representatives; or if, before that day, the President of the Senate resigns by giving to the Secretary-General to the Senate a written notice of resignation, with the consent of the President of the Senate, becomes the holder of another public office, 52 Constitution (Amendment) — of 2026 would, if he or she were a member of the House of Representatives, vacate his or her place by reason of the operation of section 70, is absent from 2 consecutive sittings of the Senate, is nominated as a candidate for the election to the House of Representatives, is appointed as Attorney-General, or is removed from office by a resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members of the Senate.

The office of Vice-President of the Senate becomes vacant if the Vice-President resigns by giving to the President of the Senate a written notice of resignation, vacates his or her place in the Senate, is appointed as Attorney-General, or is removed from office by a resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members of the Senate.

FICAC will no longer exist if Constitution Amendment Bill is passed FICAC Act to be repealed By Vijay Narayan 30/09/2026 The Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption will no longer exist if the Constitution Amendment Bill is passed.

FICAC is not included in the proposed Constitution tabled by Prime Minister, Sitiveni Rabuka.

The repeal of the FICAC 2007 is also stated in the Bill.

The Constitution Amendment Bill will be debated on Friday and the third reading of the Bill is expected to take place in 30 days.

Constitution Bill sets out proposed equality and discrimination provisions By Rashika Kumar 01/10/2026 The Constitution Amendment Bill states that a person must not be unfairly discriminated against, directly or indirectly, on grounds including race, culture, ethnic or social origin, colour, place of origin, sex, gender, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, birth, primary language, economic or social or health status, disability, age, religion, conscience, marital status or pregnancy. The Bill tabled by Prime Minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, focuses on equality before the law and protection against discrimination where every person would be equal before the law and have the right to equal protection, treatment and benefit of the law. The Bill states that equality includes the full and equal enjoyment of all rights and freedoms recognised in the Constitution or any other written law. The provision also covers discrimination based on opinions or beliefs, except where those opinions or beliefs involve harm to others or the diminution of the rights or freedoms of others. The Bill states that a law or administrative action taken under a law may not directly or indirectly impose a limitation or restriction on any person on a prohibited ground. It also states that every person has the right of access, membership or admission, without discrimination on a prohibited ground, to shops, hotels, lodging-houses, public restaurants, places of public entertainment, clubs, education institutions, public transportation services, taxis and public places. The proprietor of a place or service listed in the provision must facilitate reasonable access for persons with disabilities to the extent prescribed by law. The Bill states that treating one person differently from another on any of the grounds prescribed under subsection 3 is discrimination, unless it can be established that the difference in treatment is not unfair in the circumstances. The proposed provision also sets out circumstances where a law or administrative action would not be inconsistent with the rights in the equality provision. These include laws that appropriate revenues or other money for particular purposes, impose a retirement age, impose restrictions or confer privileges on people employed or engaged in State service, or impose restrictions or confer privileges on non-citizens. They also include laws relating to adoption, marriage, devolution of property on death and pensions, as well as laws excluding persons from holding certain public offices. The Bill also provides for laws or administrative actions that limit a right or freedom to the extent necessary in relation to the communal ownership of iTaukei, Rotuman and Banaban lands, access to marine resources, or the bestowing of iTaukei, Rotuman and Banaban chiefly title or rank. A law or administrative action may also limit a right or freedom for the purpose of providing for the application of the customs of iTaukei, Rotuman or the Banaban community relating to the holding, use or transmission of, or distribution of the produce of, land or fishing rights, or entitlement to any chiefly title or rank. It may also impose a restriction on the alienation of land or fishing rights held in accordance with iTaukei, Rotuman or Banaban custom, or permit the temporary alienation of that land or those rights without the consent of the owners. The Bill further states that a law or administrative action may limit a right or freedom for the purpose of providing for the governance of iTaukei or Rotuman or of the Banaban community and of other persons living as members of an iTaukei, Rotuman or Banaban community. However, subsection 11 states that such a limitation is valid only if it accords to every person to whom it applies the right to equality before the law without discrimination other than on the ground of race or ethnic origin. It must also not infringe a right or freedom set out in any other section of the Chapter. Debate on the Constitution Amendment Bill will take place in Parliament tomorrow.

Constitution Bill guarantees freedom of speech, publication and access to information with certain limitations By Mansi Chand 01/10/2026 Image: Fiji Parliament The Constitution Amendment Bill tabled in Parliament proposes e very person has the right to freedom of speech, expression, thought, opinion and publication under Section 20.

This include freedom to seek, receive and impart information, knowledge and ideas, freedom of the press, including print, electronic and other media, freedom of imagination and creativity and academic freedom and freedom of scientific research.

The Bill says freedom of speech, expression, thought, opinion and publication does not protect— propaganda for war, incitement to violence or insurrection against this Constitution ; or 24 Constitution (Amendment) of 2026 advocacy of hatred that is based on any prohibited ground of discrimination listed or prescribed under section 29 and constitutes incitement to cause harm.

It stresses that a law may limit, or may authorise the limitation of the rights and freedoms in the interests of national security, public safety, public order, public morality, public health or the orderly conduct of elections, the protection or maintenance of the reputation, privacy, dignity, rights or freedoms of other persons, including the right to be free from hate speech, whether directed against individuals or groups and the rights of persons injured by inaccurate or offensive media reports to have a correction published on reasonable conditions established by law, preventing the disclosure, as appropriate, of information received in confidence, preventing attacks on the dignity of individuals, groups of individuals or respected offices or institutions in a manner likely to promote ill will between ethnic or religious groups or the oppression of, or discrimination against, any person or group of persons, maintaining the authority and independence of the courts; imposing reasonable restrictions on the holders of public offices in order to secure their impartial and confidential service, and regulating the technical administration of telecommunications.

The Bill states that in this section, “hate speech” means an expression in whatever form that encourages, or has the effect of encouraging discrimination on a ground listed or prescribed under section 29.

Meanwhile, the Bill states e very person has the right of access to information held by any public office.

The Bill says every person has the right to the correction or deletion of untrue or misleading information that affects that person.

item.title: More than 50 leaders, Ministers and negotiators gather in Nadi for Pre-COP31
item.description: Fiji is putting Pacific priorities and solutions at the centre of global climate discussions as more than 50 countries gather in the country from today for the 2026 Pacific Pre-COP meeting. Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says we know the science have spoken, our own eyes have seen and he says he knows, doing nothing is no longer neutral, it is a choice.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji is putting Pacific priorities and solutions at the centre of global climate discussions as more than 50 countries gather in the country from today for the 2026 Pacific Pre-COP meeting.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says we know the science have spoken, our own eyes have seen and he says he knows, doing nothing is no longer neutral, it is a choice.

The Prime Minister is asking the leaders who come to our shores to see, and listen with an open heart to those of us on the front line and to come ready to accelerate and deliver the effort needed to keep our promise, to honour our shared moral and legal obligation to limit global average temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius.

He says every fraction of a degree of human-driven warming moves us beyond the balance set by God's creation and inflicts further harm on homes and villages and livelihoods.

Rabuka is asking world leaders and Ministers to come with the courage to face down the forest-filled addictions and greed that continues to fuel this crisis, for we cannot, in good faith, allow it to unfold and grow any further.

Traditional fishing grounds could be lost if global temperatures overshoot 1.5 degrees “ Dr Varea By Rashika Kumar 04/10/2026 Traditional fishing grounds could be lost if global temperatures overshoot 1.5 degrees Celsius, as fish are forced to move to new feeding grounds, according to Pacific Islands Climate Action Network Director Dr Rufino Varea. While speaking to fijivillage News, Dr Varea says an overshoot scenario could see customary and traditional fishing grounds lost as fish move to newer feeding grounds. He says natural cycles would also be disrupted, affecting spawning and breeding seasons, while practices observed and practised by traditional Pacific communities for generations could also be at risk of being lost. Dr Varea says the Pacific is already experiencing climate change impacts, although the region has not yet reached an overshoot beyond 1.5 degrees Celsius. He says the current El Niño event is contributing to some of the impacts being experienced, while continued carbon dioxide emissions from countries that produce and use large amounts of fossil fuels are warming the planet. Dr Varea says oceans and forests can absorb only a limited amount of excess emissions, and emissions are being released at a rate beyond the planet's ability to remain in balance. He says while an overshoot beyond 1.5 degrees Celsius may be temporary, some of its consequences would be permanent. Dr Varea says native forests and endemic species could be threatened with extinction when temperatures exceed 1.5 degrees, and returning below the threshold would not bring extinct species back. He says this is why the Pacific's message has always been 1.5 to stay alive. Varea says 1.5 degrees Celsius is the threshold the Pacific cannot surpass, with higher temperatures bringing increasingly severe impacts including sea level rise, mass coral bleaching, saltwater intrusion into freshwater supplies and displacement of communities. He says the Pacific's priorities at pre-COP and COP31 are centred on four thematic pillars. One of which is keeping 1.5 alive and maintaining it as the primary goal under the Paris Agreement. Varea says the International Court of Justice advisory opinion on climate change states that all states have an obligation to ensure they keep 1.5 degrees as the primary goal under the Paris Agreement. The second priority is climate finance, with Dr Varea calling for more simplified and accessible finance to flow into the Pacific so communities can receive the support needed to respond to climate change. Dr Varea says the Pre-COP31 coming to the Pacific provides an opportunity to bring the stories and lived experiences of frontline communities into international discussions. He says many Pacific communities do not have the funding to engage directly in the process, making it important that their voices are heard in these spaces. The Pacific Pre-COP31 starts in Nadi tomorrow and concludes on Friday while COP31 will be held in Antalya, Turkiye next month.

Dramasi women wake up at 2am to collect water as climate change dries up water sources By Rashika Kumar 04/10/2026 Women in Dramasi, Tavua are waking up as early as 2 or 3 in the morning and climbing over a hill to collect water as climate change continues to dry up water sources in the community. Pacific Centre for Peacebuilding Executive Director Florence Swamy says the women have to collect water during the night because if they wait until the sun comes up, animals go to the water source and contaminate it. She says the water source is a river or small creek, but the impact of prolonged dry conditions is clear, with some of the creeks in Dramasi now so dry that they look like roads. Swamy says women have to carry the water back to their homes, adding to the pressure they already face every day. She says the women the Centre worked with, aged between about 21 and 65, would start their day at around 4.30 or 5 in the morning by preparing breakfast and lunch for the men before they leave for the farms, gold mines in Vatukoula or odd jobs around Tavua and Ba. She says the women then prepare their children for school, complete household work, tend to market gardens around their homes and meet their community obligations. Swamy says their days can continue until around 10.30 or 11 at night, before some women wake again at 2 or 3 in the morning to collect water. She says the lack of water is affecting hygiene, including how women teach young girls about hygiene, as well as water for daily use and market gardening. Swamy says this has become a food security issue because women can no longer rely on their gardens to provide food, which can then affect the health and well-being of families. She says access to the community is also becoming a problem, as roads have not been properly maintained and commercial water suppliers have stopped going to the area because the condition of the roads is damaging their vehicles. Swamy says one of the women, Urmila Prasad, is also an advisory councillor and is actively raising the concerns of the community with authorities. She says the Centre has also brought women from Dramasi together with women from nearby Korovou to form a joint multicultural and multi-ethnic network. Swamy says the network gives the women a platform to collectively raise issues with authorities, including water, which is a concern for both Indo-Fijian and iTaukei women. She says the women are already demonstrating leadership in their homes, and the network is helping them amplify their needs and take leadership in addressing issues affecting their communities. Swamy says the challenges in Dramasi are not limited to climate change, as the community is also a sugarcane farming community facing the existing pressures in the sugar industry. She says young people are also leaving the community to look for work elsewhere, with labour migration bringing additional social problems. Swamy says older people are increasingly looking after their grandchildren because their parents have left to find work, sometimes for long periods, and in some cases money does not come back. She says this leaves older people relying on limited social welfare support to care for their grandchildren. Swamy says the Centre worked with about 16 women from 12 households in Dramasi as part of its Women’s Peacebuilding Leadership Programme and Climate Change and Conflict Programme. She says the Centre has also worked with women in nearby Korovou, where livelihoods are being affected by the loss of mangroves and declining crab catches. Swamy says the women in Korovou traditionally relied on crabbing for their livelihoods, but mangroves are being cut down and ecosystems are being destroyed, resulting in fewer crabs. She says the women are now having to go further into the sea and spend longer periods standing in the water to catch enough crabs to sell. Swamy says this is affecting their physical health, including their knees, because they are spending longer periods in cold water, while exposure to the sun is also a concern. She says pollution around the expanding town is another problem, with flooding carrying waste into the mangroves and affecting marine life. Swamy says the women from the two communities are now working together through their joint network, allowing them to bring different strengths and concerns together and collectively advocate for their communities. She says the Centre’s advocacy going into the Pacific Pre-COP31 discussions is that climate change must be viewed beyond its physical effects and the infrastructure required to respond to it. Swamy says the impacts on communities must also be considered as a human security and conflict prevention issue because as resources become scarce, competition and tensions can increase. She says communities must have access to climate financing so they can build resilience, rather than climate financing being directed only towards solutions after problems occur. Swamy says it is important that the experiences and needs of communities such as Dramasi and Korovou are reflected in discussions on climate change and climate financing. Questions have been sent to the Water Authority of Fiji regarding the water situation in Dramasi. Negotiators from about 36 countries are convening in Nadi from tomorrow until Friday for Pre-COP31 to discuss key issues ahead of COP31. The Pacific Pre-COP31 discussions will focus on four key pillars including keeping 1.5°C within reach, enhancing access to climate finance, elevating the ocean-climate nexus, and amplifying Pacific voices and leadership.

Praising resilience while expanding fossil fuels is an excuse for inaction“ Archbishop Chong By Rashika Kumar 04/10/2026 Praising Pacific Islanders for being strong and resilient while continuing to expand fossil fuels becomes a moral excuse for inaction, delaying climate finance and leaving Pacific communities to bear the consequences of an atmospheric crisis they did not cause. This has been highlighted by the Head of the Catholic Church in Fiji Archbishop Peter Loy Chong while delivering a reflection during the Ecumenical and Inter-Faith Sunday Service at the Crowne Plaza Hotel in Nadi ahead of Pre-COP31, which begins tomorrow. He says Pacific Islanders have for too long been praised for their resilience while the expansion of fossil fuels continues. Archbishop Chong says resilience is no longer enough and the world must acknowledge the vulnerability and suffering of Pacific communities. He says the theology of vulnerability demands that diplomatic and polite language is stripped away and the world honestly acknowledges the grave moral wound at the centre of the climate crisis. He says Pacific communities are hurting, their land is dry and their suffering is profoundly unjust. Archbishop Chong says global leaders and polluting industries should not stand at the foot of Pacific communitiesâ€™ suffering and admire how bravely they carry the burden of climate change. He stresses it is a sin before the Creator for wealthy nations and extractive industries to applaud the sacrifice of Pacific communities while granting new drilling licences, burning more coal and offering empty pledges. Archbishop Chong says true ecological conversion demands that repentance be matched by restitution and justice. He demands uncompromising and radical reductions in emissions, full accountability for loss and damage, direct, grant-based climate finance, not loans and subsidiarity and inclusive governance, so people who are victims of climate change are invited into important climate meetings. He adds the world must turn grief into justice, vulnerability into solidarity and collective will into the salvation of the common home. Negotiators from about 36 countries are convening in Nadi from tomorrow until Friday for Pre-COP31 to discuss key issues ahead of COP31. The Pacific Pre-COP31 discussions will focus on four key pillars including keeping 1.5°C within reach, enhancing access to climate finance, elevating the ocean-climate nexus, and amplifying Pacific voices and leadership.

Doing nothing on climate change is a choice - Rabuka By Rashika Kumar 05/10/2026 As Ministers and world leaders from more than 50 countries gather in Nadi for Pacific Pre-COP31 from today, Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says we know the science have spoken, our own eyes have seen and he says he knows, doing nothing is no longer neutral, it is a choice. While speaking during the Ecumenical and Inter-Faith Sunday Service at the Crowne Plaza Hotel in Nadi, Rabuka says climate change is not only a scientific problem or an economic one, it is a moral one. While highlighting scriptures from the book of Leviticus, he says the earth is not ours to exhaust, adding it says no one should carry a burden forever, and it says, there comes a time to set things right. Rabuka stresses we carry a burden that we did not create. He says our elders never separated land from sea or people from their place of Vanua. Rabuka says the Vanua is one living whole and what wounds one part, wounds all of it. He says when the tide reaches our homes, when the reef our grandmothers knew grows pale, when a village must pack up and move to higher ground, that is not a statistic, it is a family, it is a sacred trust being broken. The Prime Minister is asking the leaders who come to our shores to see, and listen with an open heart to those of us on the front line and to come ready to accelerate and deliver the effort needed to keep our promise, to honour our shared moral and legal obligation to limit global average temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius. He says every fraction of a degree of human-driven warming moves us beyond the balance set by God's creation and inflicts further harm on homes and villages and livelihoods. Rabuka is asking world leaders and Ministers to come with the courage to face down the forest-filled addictions and greed that continues to fuel this crisis, for we cannot, in good faith, allow it to unfold and grow any further. Rabuka says Fiji and Pacific leaders will be clear over the coming days that in addition to addressing the core drivers of the climate crisis, action must be taken to tackle the impacts we already face. He says leaders and Pacific negotiators alike will deliver a clear message on the need for finance to reach the communities who need it, not someday, but now, as an act of justice, not charity. Ministers, leaders and negotiators from more that 50 countries are convening in Nadi from today until Friday for Pre-COP31 to discuss key issues and their agenda for COP31. The Pacific Pre-COP31 discussions will focus on four key pillars including keeping 1.5°C within reach, enhancing access to climate finance, elevating the ocean-climate nexus, and amplifying Pacific voices and leadership.

Pacific priorities take centre stage as Pre-COP31 begins By Priya Nand 05/10/2026 Fiji is putting Pacific priorities and solutions at the centre of global climate discussions as more than 50 countries gather in the country from today for the 2026 Pacific Pre-COP meeting. Minister for Information, Environment and Climate Change Lynda Tabuya says the Pacific’s influence on global climate action has always been greater than its size. Tabuya says Pre-COP will help turn climate commitments into practical action, including securing greater investment in blue economy solutions to protect the oceans. She says renewable energy strengthens resilience, reduces fuel costs and supports sustainable development across the region. Pre-COP is being co-hosted by Fiji and Australia from today until Thursday, while a special Leaders’ event will take place in Tuvalu from today to tomorrow. The meeting is the last major Ministerial meeting before COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye. Keeping the 1.5 degrees Celsius target within reach, accelerating the clean energy transition, safeguarding the ocean and unlocking finance for vulnerable countries will be key areas of discussion. The meeting comes as climate-related disasters including glacier collapse, heatwaves and tropical storms continue to affect millions of people around the world. The organisers say collective action has already brought projected global warming down from four degrees Celsius to 2.6 degrees, following the Paris Agreement in 2015. International Energy Agency figures show renewables now account for more than 34 percent of electricity generation worldwide, compared with 23 percent in 2015. Renewables are also now the cheapest form of energy generation globally and the fastest to deploy, with twice as much renewable capacity forecast to be installed from 2025 to 2030 compared with 2019 to 2024. Fiji will also host the Vale ni Vanua Knowledge Exchange programme, highlighting youth climate leadership, the latest climate science and solutions to climate impacts in maternal health, the ocean and agriculture. Meanwhile, Tuvalu’s Minister for Climate Change and the Environment, Dr Maina Vakafua Talia says the Leaders’ event will bring global decision-makers to the frontlines of climate change and show the impacts faced by communities. He says Tuvalu is a low-lying atoll nation, with an average height of just two metres above sea level, and decisions made at Pre-COP and COP31 will be felt by its communities first. Australian Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen says the Pacific is at the frontline of the climate crisis, where the effects of climate change are real and immediate. Bowen says hosting Pre-COP in the Pacific is bringing global attention to the impacts, opportunities and priorities of the region. COP31 President and Türkiye’s Minister for Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Murat Kurum says promises do not hold back the sea or shield homes from fire, and only delivery can save people. Kurum says the COP31 Presidency has an action plan covering electrification, zero waste, resilient cities and oceans, all supported by finance. He says the aim is to have the world arrive in Antalya ready to deliver results. Over the four days, leaders and delegates will take part in sessions and bilateral meetings focused on climate action, clean energy, investment and resilience.

Pacific must be at centre of global climate decision-making – Tabuya By Rashika Kumar 05/10/2026 Climate decisions are only as strong as the voices that shape them. This has been highlighted by Minister for Environment Lynda Tabuya while opening the Pacific Pre-COP31 at Sofitel Resort, where she has stressed that we have to be present to be heard. The Minister is appealing to COP President and co-chair to join Fiji and the Pacific as they lobby to get the oceans on the climate agenda. Tabuya stresses that the Pacific must continue to fight to protect Na Moana, the ocean. She is urging people to tell the leaders plainly what further warming would mean for their communities, and show them where finance is failing, and where it is working. Australia’s Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen says the leaders must use COP31 to elevate the views and the experiences of the Pacific in the COP processes, which have not been heard strongly enough in the past. He says no one is more important in that process than the Pacific. Bowen stresses that the Pacific, which has done so little to cause climate change, and has so much at stake in combating climate change. The Australian Minister says there are four nations in the world that, on a sober reading of the projections, face the very real risk of being submerged and 3 of them are here in the Pacific. Bowen says 34 leaders, influential people, presidents of multilateral development banks, will be going to Tuvalu tomorrow to lift the profile of these issues on the world stage . He says the fact that some of the nations that need climate finance for adaptation the most are those who struggle to get it the hardest and the fact that oceans, which are so important in terms of the potential outcomes, the potential mitigation, but also the impacts, have not featured so strongly in public negotiations in years past. He says that Fiji is again calling on the world to match ambition with delivery. Bowen says Australia is a proud member of the Pacific family and shares the region, ocean and future with Pacific countries. He says the work being done at Pre-COP31 is important as countries seek to build consensus across more than 190 parties ahead of COP31 in Antalya. Bowen says Australia will leave no stone unturned to ensure the Pacific’s voices are heard and that COP31 delivers meaningful progress. He says the COP must focus on implementation and acceleration, including delivering on renewable energy and energy efficiency commitments. Bowen says he is confident COP31 will be remembered as a meeting where the world took a forward step and recognised that multilateralism matters more than ever. He says it should also be remembered as a COP where a region that has not had its voices heard strongly enough, like the Pacific, has its voices heard by the end of the conference. Ministers, leaders and negotiators from more that 50 countries are convening in Nadi from today until Friday for Pre-COP31 to discuss key issues and their agenda for COP31. Hosted by Australia in Fiji and Tuvalu, the Pacific Pre-COP31 discussions will focus on four key pillars including keeping 1.5°C within reach, enhancing access to climate finance, elevating the ocean-climate nexus, and amplifying Pacific voices and leadership.

Remote and maritime schools to receive solar power with AUD$1M assistance By Rashika Kumar 05/10/2026 Schools in remote and maritime areas are expected to be equipped with solar energy as Australia has announced AUD$1 million for the It's Time Foundation to work with the Fiji's Ministry of Education. This has been announced by Australian Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen while speaking during a press conference with Minister for Environment Lynda Tabuya during Pacific COP31 at Sofitel Resort in Denarau. Bowen says this is the sort of practical action that Australia takes to help the Pacific transition away from fossil fuels. While responding to a question by fijivillage News on what assurance can Fiji and the Pacific get that our voices will be heard during COP31 negotiations as Australia remains a coal and gas exporter, Bowen says the way to transition away from fossil fuels is to build more renewable energy, to replace the need for fossil fuel and that is what they are doing in Australia. Bowen says Australia's increased use of home batteries has reduced gas demand, while the country is building renewable energy capacity to replace coal-fired power. He says Australia, despite accounting for only 1 percent of global emissions, can work with other countries to address the remaining 99 percent and support a transition away from fossil fuels by tackling both demand and supply. Meanwhile, in response to Australian media questioning Bowen on Australian taxpayers money, Tabuya says the Pacific is grateful for Australia's support and for helping Fiji and Tuvalu host Pre-COP31. She says Pacific countries may disagree with Australia on some issues, but it is important to find common ground and agree on action going into COP31. Bowen has reassured that Pacific Climate Ministers will meet with him every day during COP31 to be updated on negotiations, obstacles and challenges and to discuss the way forward. He says Pacific Ministers will be part of the process and will not be called into discussions only after agreements have already been reached. Bowen says he cannot guarantee that the COP31 decision will reflect everything Pacific Ministers want, as negotiations involve around 190 countries and require consensus. He says the process will require goodwill, flexibility and pragmatism, but the Pacific will be more at the table than it has been at a COP before. Tabuya adds the Pacific is grateful for Australia's commitment to renewable energy. She says many Pacific communities are not connected to the electricity grid and have an opportunity to move directly to renewable energy rather than relying on fossil fuels. Tabuya says Fiji is calling on Australia and the international community to support the Pacific through climate finance and projects that will enable a just transition away from fossil fuels. She says developed countries must commit to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and support countries that are most affected by climate change. Pre-COP continues throughout the week, with more than 35 Ministers, leaders and other delegates going to Tuvalu tomorrow, with discussions resuming in Fiji from Wednesday until Friday.

Pacific women face loss, displacement and deepening poverty due to climate change - Nabulivou By Rashika Kumar 05/10/2026 Pacific women and girls are facing loss and damage, displacement, gender-based violence and deepening poverty as the impacts of climate change intensify. This has been highlighted by Diva for Equality Director Noelene Nabulivou during the Pacific Pre-COP31 Opening Plenary Session at Sofitel Resort in Denarau. Nabulivou says Pacific women and communities are experiencing irreversible impacts on indigenous land, waterways and food systems, while climate change is also contributing to forced displacement and heightened gender-based violence. She says women are also confronting patriarchal and ecocidal forces that exploit communities, the environment and the ocean. Nabulivou says Pacific women are calling for urgent climate action, including a just phase-out of fossil fuels, climate finance based on the 1.5-degree Celsius target and stronger gender-responsive climate policies. She says compromising on the 1.5-degree Celsius threshold could have devastating consequences for frontline Pacific communities. Nabulivou says women and gender-diverse people must be placed at the centre of climate decision-making as governments work towards COP31. Ministers, leaders and negotiators from more that 50 countries are convening in Nadi from today until Friday for Pre-COP31 to discuss key issues and their agenda for COP31. Hosted by Australia in Fiji and Tuvalu, the Pacific Pre-COP31 discussions focuses on four key pillars including keeping 1.5°C within reach, enhancing access to climate finance, elevating the ocean-climate nexus, and amplifying Pacific voices and leadership.

Pacific can now demand climate action as a legal obligation – Shaheed By Rashika Kumar 06/10/2026 The Pacific can now approach climate negotiations from a stronger position by demanding climate action as a legal obligation rather than simply asking for assistance. This has been highlighted by Pacific Islands Students Fighting Climate Change Engagement and Outreach Lead Abdul Mufeez Shaheed during a panel discussion on the sidelines of the Pacific Pre-COP31 in Nadi. Shaheed says the International Court of Justice advisory opinion has given the Pacific greater legal clarity and a stronger position in climate negotiations. He says they go into COP, they go into negotiations with a much stronger position, where they no longer talk about losing their home if nothing happens but can now say that they are required by law to do this. Shaheed says climate change is not simply a political issue for Pacific communities, but an issue affecting human rights, livelihoods, culture, homes and future generations . He says the ICJ has clarified that states have a duty to prevent significant harm to the climate system and that where states fail to act, there must be a remedy. Shaheed says the next step is to ensure climate harm experienced by communities is properly documented. He says the impacts of climate change are often felt most by women, girls, young people and marginalised communities, and these experiences need to form part of how climate harm is assessed. He stresses our stories are not decorations for a panel but are evidence. Shaheed says every nationally determined contribution, national adaptation plan and climate law in the Pacific should be tested against the ICJ advisory opinion. He says young people should be involved as co-authors in developing these policies rather than being brought in only for consultation. Shaheed says the focus must now be on ensuring the legal clarity provided by the ICJ reaches communities.

Nawajikuma families face repeated flooding, call for better drainage and river protection By Rashika Kumar 07/10/2026 Families in Nawajikuma Settlement in Nadi continue to face flooding caused by poor drainage, rising river levels and soil erosion, with residents having to move to an evacuation centre when water level rises. 64-year-old Vasiti Vosawale Lesavua, who lives in Nawajikuma Settlement near Nawaka, says flooding has become a major challenge for the densely populated settlement, which is home to about 100 families or about 400 to 500 people. Lesavua says the settlement is easily affected by floods because of poor drainage, while the Nadi River and Nawaka River also contribute to flooding during natural disasters. She says the development of the back road has also contributed to the flooding, while water from the Nawaka River can come from behind the settlement without residents realising it is rising. Lesavua says residents often focus on the Nadi River, but flooding from the Nawaka River can come with great force and cause significant damage. She says when the river level starts rising or there is heavy rain, she tells her children to collect what they need in their school bags, along with food and containers to collect water. Lesavua says residents usually move to Saint Andrews Primary School, which serves as an evacuation centre. She says the situation becomes particularly dangerous at night when residents have to cross the main Nadi Back Road to reach the evacuation centre. Lesavua says there was an incident when the water level was so high that residents could not cross the road, forcing people to cling to a rope placed across the road to reach the other side. She says it is very risky because residents cannot carry their belongings when the water level is high. Lesavua says flooding usually occurs during the cyclone season from November to April or when there is heavy rain, and it can happen about twice a year depending on rainfall. She says climate change is also contributing to the problem , with soil erosion causing the river to become wider and the river banks to become lower. Lesavua says trees along the river banks have also been cut down, while bamboo that once helped protect the banks has been washed away. She says heavier rainfall then contributes to further erosion, landslides and flooding, allowing water to enter the settlement. She says many residents have limited financial capacity, with most people earning only enough to meet their daily subsistence needs. Lesavua says this makes it difficult for families to save enough money to raise their houses and foundations to protect themselves from flooding. Speaking to fijivillage during Pre-COP31, Lesavua says she wants leaders and ministers to understand the challenges faced by communities such as Nawajikuma and provide support. She is calling for a better drainage system as the settlement has two rivers and a drain running between them. Lesavua is also calling for some form of man-made river bank or a wall along the back river to help prevent soil erosion and reduce flooding. She says there are many organisations willing to assist, but they first need to know about the challenges communities are facing. Lesavua says raising the issue at Pre-COP31 could help bring attention and support to Nawajikuma. She says participating in Pre-COP31 has been an eye-opener for her and she is thankful to the Pacific Centre for Peacebuilding for allowing her to participate.

Fiji commits US$10M to Pacific Resilience Facility By Rashika Kumar 07/10/2026 Fiji has committed US$10 million to the Pacific Resilience Facility, strengthening its contribution to a regional fund aimed at helping Pacific countries respond to the impacts of climate change.

This has been announced by Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka during the Pacific Pre-COP in Nadi.

He confirmed the amount will be facilitated over a 5-year period.

Australian Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen welcomed the contribution, saying the Pacific Resilience Facility is designed by the Pacific for the Pacific.

Bowen also announced a AUS$3 million contribution to the Climate Infrastructure for Resilient Coastlines and Riverbanks project, which will support climate-resilient infrastructure in Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Kiribati and Tuvalu.

Minister for Environment and Climate Change Lynda Tabuya says Fiji’s contribution demonstrates that Pacific countries are not simply asking the international community for assistance, but are also investing in their own resilience.

Tabuya says Fiji is committed to helping itself while calling on global partners to invest in the Pacific Resilience Facility.

The facility has a target of US$500 million.

Tabuya says the Pacific is united in taking its priorities to COP31, including keeping global warming within the 1.5 degrees Celsius limit.

She says the impacts of climate change are already being experienced across the Pacific, including through sea level rise, coastal erosion and damage to infrastructure.

Tabuya says Fiji’s US$10 million commitment is part of the Pacific’s effort to build its own resilience while encouraging greater international support.

Bowen says the Pacific Resilience Facility is being built step by step through contributions from countries around the world.

He says Australia’s additional $3 million commitment will support four projects, including upgrades to the Kings Road and Queens Road in Fiji.

Tabuya says some coastal roads in Fiji will need to be repaired, while others may eventually need to be relocated because of climate impacts.

She says Fiji will also need to contribute from its own national budget towards relocation and other resilience work.

A special fijivillage Straight Talk Public Forum with Vijay Narayan focuses on the theme, Online Safety: Connected and Protected?

Joining the panel are Online Safety Commissioner Filipe Batiwale and Fiji Law Reform Commissioners David Solvalu and Valerie Narain.

WATCH: Special fijivillage Straight Talk Public Forum on Online Safety By fijivillage 28/08/2026 A special fijivillage Straight Talk Public Forum with Vijay Narayan on the theme of the forum is Online Safety: Connected and Protected?

The panelists for the public forum are Online Safety Commissioner, Filipe Batiwale, Fiji Law Reform Commissioners David Solvalu and Valerie Narain.

The Straight Talk forum focuses on Online Safety Issues in Fiji, what is being faced by the Online Safety Commission, the feedback from the members of the public during the consultation process on the review of the Online Safety Act 2018, the call for age restrictions for Social Media, the response from victims, the changes being proposed and the reasons behind them amongst other issues.

Online Safety Commission calls for stronger laws and adequate budgets to ensure victims get justice By Vijay Narayan 01/09/2026 As online harms become more serious in Fiji, the Online Safety Commission stresses that we need to keep up with stronger laws and adequate budgets to ensure the victims also get justice. Online Safety Commissioner, Filipe Batiwale says one issue being raised by the Commission during the review of the Online Safety Act is whether the Commission should have limited prosecutorial powers for specified offences under the new online-safety legislation. Commissioner Batiwale says the proposal should be considered on its merits and with appropriate safeguards. He says he understands why people may be cautious about giving a regulator more powers, but we should also be prepared to ask whether the current system is giving victims the best outcome. Batiwale says the Commission's proposal would not remove Police from serious online offending or replace the constitutional role of the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions. The Commission is proposing that consideration be given to a specialist pathway for defined offences, with separation between investigation and prosecution decisions, evidential and public-interest tests and appropriate Police, DPP and judicial oversight. The Commissioner says he is not asking for unchecked power. Batiwale says they are asking to design a system that makes sense for the kind of cases they are now dealing with. The Online Safety Commission says Fiji is dealing with more serious and complex forms of online harm, but the institutions expected to respond must be given the laws, resources and technical capability to keep pace. The Commission says it's annual budget has reduced from approximately $1.5 million to $1.1 million, at a time when the nature of complaints coming through its doors is becoming increasingly difficult. Commissioner Batiwale says the issue is not simply about the number of complaints. He says they are seeing more serious complaints now, and these are not always arguments between people on facebook. Some matters involve children, intimate images, threats, exploitation, fake accounts, multiple platforms and digital evidence that can disappear very quickly. Batiwale says t his changes the kind of response that is required from the Commission. The Online Safety Commission received 1,609 complaints in 2025, with more than half involving cyberbullying, harassment or defamatory electronic communications. About 65 percent arose on Meta platforms, particularly f acebook and Instagram. The Commission says its work increasingly requires more than simply receiving a complaint and contacting a social-media platform. They say serious cases can require evidence to be preserved, accounts to be identified, complainants to be supported, platforms to be contacted urgently and matters to be referred for criminal investigation. Commissioner Batiwale says the Commission is expected to do more as the risks become more sophisticated, while working with fewer resources. A recent reconciliation exercise between the Commission and the Fiji Police Force identified 61 matters that had been referred by the Commission for Police investigation. The Commission and Police are now working to improve how referred matters are acknowledged, tracked and progressed and how case-status information is shared between the two institutions. Commissioner Batiwale says complainants should not be left uncertain about what happens after their matter moves from the Commission to Police. The Fiji Law Reform Commission-led review of the Online Safety Act 2018 has progressed through public and stakeholder consultations and a validation process and is now in its final reporting and legislative drafting stage. The Commission says it has been contributing its experience of working under the current Act, including the problems faced when dealing with serious complaints, overseas social-media platforms, evidence, Police referrals and emerging forms of technology-facilitated abuse. Commissioner Batiwale stresses that the review of the Online Safety Act provides Fiji with an important opportunity. He says w e should not go through an entire law reform exercise and come out the other side with the same practical problems. Batiwale says if the law is strengthened, people should be able to feel the difference when they need help - t hat means looking seriously at what powers the Commission needs, what Police needs, how matters move between agencies, what obligations platforms should have and how quickly action can be taken when someone is being harmed. The Commission says it also continues to encounter difficulties when harmful content, relevant accounts or important evidence sit with multinational technology companies operating outside Fiji. Under the current Online Safety Act, the Commission does not have direct statutory authority to compel global platforms to remove harmful content. Commissioner Batiwale says that imbalance must also form part of the reform discussion. He says if a platform is happy to provide services in Fiji and benefit from Fijians using that platform, there also needs to be a reliable way for Fiji to get a response when a child, family or victim is in serious difficulty. Batiwale says we cannot have a situation where the harm is happening here but the practical ability to respond to it sits somewhere overseas. Members of the public experiencing online harm can contact the Online Safety Commission through its official complaint channels or call the toll-free assistance line 1548. Meanwhile a special fijivillage Straight Talk Public Forum with Vijay Narayan will go live at 7pm this Friday September 4th. The theme of the forum is Online Safety: Connected and Protected. The panelists for the public forum will be Online Safety Commissioner, Filipe Batiwale, and Fiji Law Reform Commissioners David Solvalu and Valerie Narain. The Straight Talk forum will focus on Online Safety Issues in Fiji, what is being faced by the Online Safety Commission, the feedback from the members of the public during the consultation process on the review of the Online Safety Act 2018, the call for age restrictions for Social Media, the response from victims, the changes being proposed and the reasons behind them amongst other issues. You can also be part of the live audience by applying for registration with a question that you would like to ask during the forum. The application to register details can be found on our website and facebook page, fijivillage. You will receive a confirmation if you have been selected to be part of the live audience. Please apply early to avoid any disappointment. The show will be broadcast live at 7pm Friday September 4th on our Facebook, YouTube and X accounts, fijivillage.

Online Safety Commission receives 960 complaints this year, 65% relate to cyberbullying By Karishma Kumari 05/09/2026 The Online Safety Commission has received about 960 complaints so far this year compared to 1,609 complaints last year, with 65 percent of the complaints relating to cyberbullying. Speaking during the fijivillage Straight Talk Public Forum with Vijay Narayan, Commissioner Filipe Batiwale says most of these complaints are being reviewed and assessed, while some have been closed off.

He says most of the cases received involve requests for electronic communications or social media posts to be taken down.

Batiwale says cyberbullying involves electronic communication being used in a way that causes harm or serious emotional distress to another person.

He adds a number of complaints remain unresolved, with one of the major issues being that complainants fail to properly complete and sign the required complaint form.

He says under the current framework, a person making a complaint to the Online Safety Commission is required to complete a form, including providing a signature, as required under the Online Safety Act regulations.

Batiwale says this requirement is sometimes overlooked by complainants and is a major drawback when dealing with complaints received by the Commission.

He says complaints can also involve people being concerned about material posted online about themselves, their relatives or other people concerned.

However, Batiwale says the Commission's current legal framework restricts its ability to assist when the online content is completely unrelated to the person making the complaint.
