He says this makes the current framework quite restrictive in terms of who can lodge a complaint with the Commission.

Further talks expected on social media ban for children in Fiji By Karishma Kumari 07/09/2026 A social media ban for children can be considered as part of the review of Fiji’s online safety laws however, further consultation, particularly with children, is needed before deciding how such restrictions would work.

Speaking on the fijivillage Straight Talk Public Forum with Vijay Narayan, Fiji Law Reform Commissioner Valerie Narain said calls for some form of social media age restriction for children came strongly from parents during their public consultation.

However, there were no clear proposals from the public on what the age restriction should be or what form a ban should take.

She says different approaches are being considered internationally, including complete bans, restrictions during certain hours and daily limits on social media use.

Narain adds they were unable to consult many children during the review process, therefore more consultation would be important if a framework for social media age restrictions is proposed.

When questioned about how authorities could police or monitor a ban if Fiji decided that children below a certain age could no longer use social media, Narain said monitoring this could be particularly difficult because children may access platforms through their parents' accounts and families may share a single device.

She says age-assurance technology also raises concerns because some systems have largely been tested on demographics outside the Pacific.

She says age verification also raises privacy concerns because adults, as well as children, may have to provide information to platforms to verify their age.

Insert: Fiji needs to consider several issues 6th Sept

When asked about what age groups should be consulted if children are to have a say on laws governing their social media use and why those age groups must be consulted, Fiji Law Reform Commissioner David Solvalu said consultations would primarily target teenagers, who are more likely to be active internet and social media users.

However, he says consultation with children would have to be conducted through their parents and most likely educational institutions, with parental consent.

Insert: Creating frameworks that are comprehensive 6th Sept

Solvalu also says the approach being considered is to create a high-level framework through primary legislation, while the technical details could then be dealt with through subsidiary legislation following further consultation.

Meanwhile, Online Safety Commisisoner Filipe Batiwale says technology is effectively the new playground for children, where they socialise, meet friends and access entertainment, and therefore it is prudent to consider their views when designing policies or frameworks governing how they communicate and live in the virtual space.

item.title: Savusavu residents raise climate concerns directly with Kamikamica at FMA Town Hall
item.description: Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says the People’s Alliance is committed to media freedom and the free flow of information. Rabuka highlighted this during the PINA Summit in Savusavu while responding to questions from fijivillage News on whether the People’s Alliance will go into the elections with a clear message to guard media independence and freedom.
item.content:encoded:
Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says the People’s Alliance is committed to media freedom and the free flow of information.

Rabuka highlighted this during the PINA Summit in Savusavu while responding to questions from fijivillage News on whether the People’s Alliance will go into the elections with a clear message to guard media independence and freedom.

The Prime Minister says the repeal of the media legislation was not for the Government, but for the people, to restore the free flow of communication between the people, the media and the rest of the world.

Rabuka says while the repeal appeared significant to the media, it was small compared with what happened in 1987.

He says about 10 years later, Her Majesty received him at the palace, but the authors of the media decree have not been able to speak to him face to face about it.

Rabuka says this shows the difference in their attitude towards what they do and what they bring into being.

The Prime Minister further says the Pacific should not silence its media because the free flow of information benefits the public, governments and news organisations.

He says open discussion is part of the Pacific way, adding that they talk and do not stop anybody from talking.

Rabuka says they do not want to silence the media and that the media should keep talking.

Asked about restrictions facing a newspaper in Samoa, Rabuka says Fiji’s experience showed that restricting the media was like operating in a dark house, as such restrictions deny people and governments information that benefits them both.

Vunidogoloa villagers in Vanua Levu are still waiting for answers on several basic infrastructure and welfare needs, 12 years after the community was relocated from its original coastal site.

Former Vunidogoloa headman Sailosi Ramatu raised the concerns during the Pre-COP31 Climate Change Town Hall Forum at Nukubalavu Village in Savusavu this evening, saying the community has repeatedly sought Government assistance but has received no response on several of the issues.

Vunidogoloa was relocated about 2 kilometres inland from its original site in 2014, with coastal erosion among the factors that contributed to the relocation.

Ramatu says the drainage system at the new site was established during the relocation, but had not been maintained.

He warns that inadequate drainage could lead to further erosion at the new site.

Ramatu also raised concerns about the lack of proper access for elderly residents and people with disabilities, particularly during emergencies.

Insert: Ramatu - We are concerned for the elderly Sept 23

Another concern is the community church, which Ramatu says was supposed to be included in the relocation package.

He says residents had contributed around $260,000 of their own money towards completing the church, despite it having been included in the Government-funded relocation package.

Ramatu adds that the community has no proper ground or playground at the new site, which he describes as important for maintaining traditional practices and providing a safe space for young people.

He says the community had also been waiting for a proper farm road, which is particularly important because many residents now rely on farming for their livelihoods.

Ramatu says the community had been raising the farm road issue with Government for about 12 years but had still not received a response.

He says the community had spent close to $600,000 supporting aspects of the relocation process and is now seeking Government assistance to address the remaining needs.

Ramatu also called for the community hall to be extended so it can serve as an evacuation centre, particularly for elderly residents and people with disabilities.

When reiterated byÂ fijivillage News Director and Fijian Media Association Executive Vijay Narayan Â that there had been no response after 12 years, Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica says previous community relocations had been carried out in an ad hoc manner.

Kamikamica says an Auditor-General's report had highlighted issues with some earlier relocations.

He says Government has since developed a standard operating procedure to improve the way future relocations are carried out.

Kamikamica says relocation was not simply about physically moving people, but also had to consider cultural, spiritual and practical needs.

Minister for Rural and Maritime Development and Disaster Management Mosese Bulitavu says some of the issues raised by Ramatu, including farm roads, churches, playgrounds and accessibility for people with disabilities, had not been adequately considered in the original relocation package.

Bulitavu says the Government has since reviewed its standard operating procedure for the relocation trust fund and incorporated lessons from previous relocation projects.

item.content:encoded:
The Constitution Review Commission Report has been tabled during a special sitting of Parliament.

Cabinet has said the tabling of the report does not constitute acceptance or adoption of all the Commission’s recommendations.

Meanwhile, Speaker of Parliament Filimone Jitoko says the report is tabled for information only and will not be referred to any Parliamentary Committee.

He also paid tribute to the late Minister for Employment, Agni Deo Singh, who passed away earlier this month.

The Parliament also held a moment of silence to honour the late Minister.

Prime Minister Sitiveni RabukaÂ believes the Government currently has the numbers required to secure the two-third parliamentary support needed for proposed constitutional changes.

While responding to fijivillage News on whether he is confident in securing two-thirds support for a bill to amend the Constitution, Rabuka said, â€œAt the moment, yes.”

When asked on theÂ proposed constitutional amendment that would limit a Prime Minister to two terms, and would rule him out from serving as Prime Minister after the next elections, Rabuka says the Bill will be debated and voted on again.Â

Rabuka also clarified that the recommendations made by the Constitution Review Commission Report are not the final proposed amendments that will go before Parliament.

He says a Cabinet sub-committee has been deliberating on the CRCâ€™s proposed amendments over the past two weeks and making changes.

The Prime Minister says those changes will be the ones that make their way to Parliament.

However, when questioned on whether there would be enough time to prepare for and hold the next general elections under a new Constitution if the proposed changes come into effect by December 24th, Rabuka, says if the Constitution is changed, transition provisions will determine which Constitution or electoral law the election will be held under.

When asked why the constitutional changes were being pursued now rather than during the Governmentâ€™s first or second year in office, Rabuka says an attempt was made in the second year but it was defeated in Parliament.

He says the matter was then referred to the Supreme Court and the process has continued.

Rabuka also rejected suggestions that the constitutional review process is being rushed.

He says he and the leadership of the National Federation Party have been talking about changing the Constitution since after 2013.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says the Government remains committed to holding the next general elections by 6th February next year, with no legal basis for a one-year extension.

While responding to questions by fijivillage News in Savusavu, Rabuka confirms thereÂ have been suggestions to extend the deadline for the elections, but it is outside the law.

When questioned about concerns that the constitution process is being rushed, Rabuka says they started talking about the constitution in 2013, when it was decreed into being.

He says everybody were talking about it, and everybody who had spoken about it should have come forward during the consultation.

Rabuka adds the result of the consultation is what they are now taking through Parliament.

He also says that the recommendations in the Constitution Review Commission's report are not the final proposed amendments that will go before Parliament.

item.description: FICAC lawyer Joseph Work says they have finalised the agreed facts and documents in former Deputy Prime Minister Professor Biman Prasad trial. Work says the trial will include both documentary and oral evidence. He says all relevant documents has been disclosed to the defence. Professor Prasad’s lawyer Richard Naidu says there are no issues and he is satisfied with the documents disclosed by the p
item.content:encoded:
FICAC lawyer Joseph Work says they have finalised the agreed facts and documents in former Deputy Prime Minister Professor Biman Prasad trial. Work says the trial will include both documentary and oral evidence. He says all relevant documents has been disclosed to the defence. Professor Prasad’s lawyer Richard Naidu says there are no issues and he is satisfied with the documents disclosed by the prosecution.

Both parties are ready for trial which is scheduled from 10th to 14th August. The matter has been adjourned to 3rd August for the final pre-trial conference before the trial. Professor Prasad has been charged by FICAC with two offences relating to alleged non-disclosure in his 2015 statutory declaration as an office holder of the National Federation Party. FICAC alleges that on or about 30th December 2015, Professor Prasad failed to declare his directorship in Platinum Hotels & Resorts PTE Limited in his declaration of assets, liabilities and income submitted to the Registrar of Political Parties, allegedly breaching the Political Parties Act. He is also charged with providing false information in a statutory declaration, with FICAC claiming that the omission of the directorship made the declaration materially false.

Former Deputy Prime Minister Professor Biman Prasad's lawyer Richard Naidu says FICAC is twisting and turning in its attempts to have a disputed document admitted as evidence in the trial.

The disputed document relates to Platinum Hotels and Resorts PTE Limited and contains details of the company's directors and secretary.

Naidu argues that the document is hearsay and that the person who prepared it must give evidence.

He says they do not even know who prepared the document and its contents must be proven to be true.

Naidu says a hearsay document is not admissible and does not constitute the best evidence.

Meanwhile, FICAC lawyer Joseph Work says the document is not hearsay as it qualifies as a public document.

Work says the evidence does not fall under the criteria of hearsay because of the statutory nature of the document and has asked for the objection to be dismissed.

Magistrate Prasad will make his ruling at 11.30am this Friday.

Professor Prasad is charged with failure to comply with statutory disclosure requirements contrary to section 24 (5) of the Political Parties Act.

FICAC alleges that between 30th December 2015 to 31st January 2016, in Suva, being an officeholder of the National Federation Party, registered under the Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding and Disclosures) Act 2013, failed to comply with Section 24(1B)(d), by providing to the office of the registrar his declaration of assets, liabilities and income as at 31st December 2015 without disclosing his directorship in Platinum Hotels & Resorts PTE Limited thereby committing an offence contrary to section 24(5) of the said Act.

It is also alleged that on 28th January 2016 in Suva, being an office holder of a registered political party, namely the National Federation Party, recklessly provided false information in a statutory declaration submitted to the Registrar of Political Parties under Section 24 (1B) (d) of the Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding and Disclosures) Act 2013, solemnly declaring that the particular contained in his declaration of assets, liabilities and income as at 31st December 2015 were true and complete when the declaration omitted his directorship in Platinum Hotels and Resorts PTE Limited, which omission rendered the declaration false in material particular thereby committing an offence contrary to Section 27 (1) (c) of the said Act.

FICAC Investigating Officer Asenaca Niumataiwalu has told the Suva Magistrates Court that statements obtained from National Federation Party General Secretary Kamal Iyer and Registered Officer Dalip Kumar were not provided to the defence in former Deputy Prime Minister Professor Biman Prasad’s case because she did not consider them relevant.

Niumataiwalu gave evidence during the hearing after defence lawyer Richard Naidu raised concerns that FICAC had two additional documents that had not been disclosed to the court or the defence.

He had also asked if documents exist, whether they were disclosed to the defence and, if they exist, why they were not disclosed.

She told the court that she conducted two investigations involving Professor Prasad.

Niumataiwalu says FICAC Enquiry Paper 89/25 relates to the current case, in which Professor Prasad is charged with failing to comply with statutory disclosure requirements contrary to Section 24(5) of the Political Parties Act.

She says FICAC Enquiry Paper 41/24 related to a separate, similar matter involving a different company which also relates to Professor Prasad.

Niumataiwalu says when investigators went to the National Federation Party office to present a search warrant and explain the reasons for the search, Iyer used abusive language.

She says FEP 41/24 was closed by the former FICAC Commissioner and Acting Deputy Commissioner last year, but some documents from that file were used in the current matter.

Niumataiwalu says the statements of Iyer and Kumar were not included in the current matter because lawyer Tupou Draunidalo’s statement was considered sufficient.

During cross-examination, Niumataiwalu agreed with Professor Prasad's lawyer Ashish Nand that Draunidalo’s statement was taken after Professor Prasad had been charged.

Niumataiwalu also agreed with Nand that documents FICAC did not consider relevant to its case could have benefited the defence.

Following Niumataiwalu’s questioning, Naidu asked Magistrate Yogesh Prasad for a hearing in chambers regarding issues arising from the proceedings and their duties as officers of the court.

Magistrate Prasad declined the request for the parties to meet in chambers.

The matter will be called again tomorrow for submissions from FICAC counsel Joseph Work and Naidu.

Naidu further told the court that it now appeared other statements may also exist and questioned what other potentially relevant material could be contained in the closed FEP 41/24 file.

He says the issue is therefore no longer limited to the two statements because the defence does not know what other material may exist that could be relevant or assist Prasad's defence.

Naidu says the matter raises broader questions about FICAC's handling of potentially relevant evidence and its disclosure obligations.

item.content:encoded:
The Fijian Teachers Association maintains that 26 teachers are affected by the Acting Heads of Schools issue, despite the Ministry of Education saying that only seven names were discussed during a meeting with teacher unions.

FTA General Secretary Paula Manumanunitoga says the Ministry acknowledged during their meeting that mistakes had been made and should now focus on rectifying the issue rather than disputing the number of affected teachers.

When fijivillage News asked whether the 7 names provided to the Ministry represented the actual number of affected teachers rather than the 26 previously stated, Manumanunitoga maintained that 26 teachers are affected.

He says the Ministry is now trying to defend its position, despite acknowledging during the meeting that mistakes had been made.

He adds that a position becomes vacant when the substantive post holder leaves the position, including through resignation, migration or death, and the Ministry can appoint someone to act while it works to permanently fill the vacancy.

Manumanunitoga says the Ministry should advertise a vacant position within six months and claims some of the affected teachers had remained in acting positions well beyond that period.

He claims some teachers had been acting in their positions for three to four years.

Manumanunitoga says mistakes can happen within the system and the matter should now be dealt with professionally and rectified after being raised by the Association.

Earlier, Permanent Secretary for Education Navin Raj said that the issue relates to 7 teachers and not 26 as reported in the media.

Raj says he met with the General Secretaries of the two teacher unions and the Ministry's Human Resources team, where 7 names were discussed after the information was verified with the FTA General Secretary.

He says acting appointments are not permanent and can be revoked once a substantive post holder is identified to fill a vacant position.

Raj says they also discussed advertising the vacant positions in due course, and he will continue consulting the General Secretaries of the two teacher unions throughout the process.

Meanwhile, Minister for Education Aseri Radrodro says the revocation of acting Headteacher appointments in the Suva Education District is an operational matter and the Ministry is reviewing the appointments in consultation with teacher unions.

Insert: Radrodro on 26 Revoke 28th Aug 26

Radrodro says Fiji has more than 730 primary schools requiring Headteacher positions, while there are 190 secondary schools that also require school heads.

He says resignations, transfers, retirements and teachers leaving the service for other opportunities continue to create vacancies that need to be filled.

Radrodro says he has directed the Appointment Secretary to address the vacancies as soon as possible while following the required human resource recruitment process.

FTA General Secretary Paula Manumanunitoga says the unions are disappointed with the Ministry's advertisement published on Saturday , August 29th.

The Fiji Education Management Information System (FEMIS) is a web-based application developed by the Ministry of Education, Heritage and Arts (MoEHA) in Fiji.

He says interested applicants are unsure about which schools they want to apply to because key information about the advertised vacancies was not included.

Manumanunitoga is questioning why the complete list of schools could not have been included in the newspaper advertisement instead of requiring teachers to access FEMIS for further details.

He says many aspiring and eligible candidates could miss out if they face internet connectivity issues and are unable to access FEMIS.

The FTA General Secretary says this is particularly concerning as teachers are currently on school holidays, with some spending their break in villages and maritime areas where internet access may be limited.

He says requiring teachers to cross-reference FEMIS unnecessarily complicates the process and is calling on the Ministry to simplify it by publishing complete advertisements containing the school names, locations, post advertisement numbers and other relevant details.

fijivillage News has contacted the Ministry of Education for a response.

Opposition MP Premila Kumar says Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka should consider replacing Education Minister Aseri Radrodro if he cannot resolve what she describes as recurring salary and allowance issues affecting teachers and their pay.

Kumar says teachers should not have to chase the Government for money they have already earned and should not be punished for administrative failures within the Ministry of Education.

She says teachers were paid only up to Pay 18, with payments subsequently stopped after a Ministry audit reportedly found that some signed contracts had not been returned.

Kumar has questioned where the systems and people responsible for ensuring these contracts are properly processed are.

She says there are Heads of Schools and Divisional Heads in all four divisions, and if administrative problems are occurring on this scale, they should have been identified and resolved earlier.
